item.title: ScienceDaily: Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder
item.description: Scientists discovered that vitamin B12 largely reversed developmental abnormalities in worms carrying a genetic mutation linked to Verheij syndrome, a rare disorder that causes growth problems and developmental delays. Similar metabolic changes were identified in human patients, raising the possibility that this common vitamin could inspire new treatments for rare genetic diseases.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover that the heart doesn't age the way we thought
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the heart ages unevenly, with surprising hotspots of inflammation and scarring concentrated in the valves and major blood vessels rather than the heart muscle. The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about cardiac aging and could help researchers develop new ways to protect the heart as we grow older.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
item.description: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
item.description: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
item.description: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
item.description: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

item.title: Nature: As El Niño builds, studies of extreme marine heatwaves must start now
item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03715-7 Researchers must track warming oceans and use the knowledge gained to inform strategies for sustaining fisheries and communities that depend on them.

item.title: Nature: The psychology of imaginary friends — and why they are good for kids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03713-9 Children often conjure up invisible pals to keep them company. A psychologist delves into the reasons why.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that when and how often older adults nap could reveal hidden warning signs about their health. Researchers followed 1,338 people for up to 19 years and discovered that longer, more frequent naps were linked to higher mortality, while morning nappers faced a 30% greater risk of death than afternoon nappers. Each additional hour of daytime sleep was associated with a 13% increase in mortality risk.

item.title: ScienceDaily: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery
item.description: A revolutionary new wearable patch could help people get more restorative sleep without medication or surgery. Developed by University of Texas researchers, the device uses gentle ultrasound to stimulate deep brain regions, helping participants enter REM sleep 43 minutes faster and remain there 16 minutes longer on average. The technology also showed promising effects on stress regulation and brain circuits involved in emotion.

item.title: ScienceDaily: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
item.description: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
item.description: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

item.title: ScienceDaily: MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
item.description: MIT scientists discovered that carefully timed bursts of gentle pink noise during sleep can strengthen the brain’s natural cleaning waves, which help flush away potentially harmful waste. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments aimed at improving sleep and memory while potentially reducing the buildup of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease.

item.title: ScienceDaily: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
item.description: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

item.title: Nature: Is the sixth great extinction imminent? Scientists must draw on natural history for clues
item.description: Nature, Published online: 16 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03712-w A lack of crosstalk between research disciplines is hampering scholars’ ability to fully examine how people have altered Earth’s biodiversity.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Are one-person firms the future of biotech?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03684-x Researchers are debating whether small, AI-enabled biotech companies are the future of drug discovery. Plus, even microplastics still reach the wildlife furthest from humanity and an upgrade to AlphaGenome.

item.title: New Scientist: The end of the universe could emerge suddenly from nothing
item.description: A bubble of absolutely nothing – truly empty space – could be out there in the cosmos. Columnist Leah Crane explores how that could exist, and the peril it puts us in

item.title: New Scientist: Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming
item.description: Clues about the diet of “Rødhals Man”, who lived some 6000 years ago, hint that he lived through one of the most revolutionary changes in human history

item.title: ScienceDaily: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
item.description: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA warns this year's Monster El Niño could be even bigger than legendary 1997 event
item.description: NASA scientists warn that the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could surpass the historic 1997-98 event, which triggered devastating weather extremes around the world. Satellite data reveal striking similarities between the two, raising the possibility of major rainfall and flooding this winter, although the exact impacts remain uncertain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
item.description: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
item.description: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
item.description: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins
item.description: A groundbreaking drone survey has revealed a startling split in the fate of New Zealand's endangered Erect-crested penguins. While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
item.description: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers
item.description: Scientists have discovered how to use flashes of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions inside a crystal, solving a decades-old mystery about how the material behaves. The laser-induced alignment lasts just a trillionth of a second, but the breakthrough could open the door to new ways of processing and storing information.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
item.description: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

item.title: ScienceDaily: AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a hidden warning sign in routine heart scans that could predict sudden cardiac death before it strikes. The AI-powered discovery outperformed conventional screening methods, potentially revealing thousands of people at risk of a fatal heart malfunction that doctors might otherwise miss.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
item.description: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome
item.description: Scientists have developed a promising new fiber supplement that improves gut health in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) without worsening bloating, pain, or other digestive symptoms. The specially designed blend also improved gut-related anxiety and produced surprisingly rapid changes in gut bacteria, potentially offering a new way to manage IBS.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered that hidden patterns of brain activity can predict Alzheimer’s risk years before memory problems appear, potentially offering an earlier warning than traditional biomarkers. The same patterns also reveal which brains are unusually resistant to aging, raising hopes for future treatments that could help protect memory.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis
item.description: A new study suggests that the right kind of exercise could help protect young adults from early knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery. Researchers found that a four-month supervised rehabilitation program improved pain, muscle strength, and quality of life without damaging knee cartilage. The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A giant icy world hiding beyond Pluto could be our sixth dwarf planet
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered a potentially enormous new dwarf planet beyond Pluto, hidden for years in one of the most crowded regions of the night sky. The discovery of 2026 ED138 could expand the solar system's official dwarf planet family and hints that more mysterious worlds may be lurking far beyond Neptune.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
item.description: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

item.title: New Scientist: New Scientist readers on how the magazine has shaped their lives
item.description: To celebrate our 70th anniversary, we asked readers how they first encountered New Scientist – and why they still read it today

item.title: ScienceDaily: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't
item.description: Yale researchers have discovered that certain prescription drugs, healthy diets, and exercise can measurably slow biological aging, while popular anti-aging supplements appear largely ineffective. Their analysis of 51 studies could transform how scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments, although whether these biological changes actually extend life remains uncertain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
item.description: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable
item.description: Smiling may not always make you happier, and new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile repeatedly could actually make you feel worse. In a University of Florida study involving more than 1,100 participants, researchers discovered that while a single artificial smile can provide a small mood boost, repeatedly faking smiles can erase that benefit or even reverse it.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
item.description: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

item.title: ScienceDaily: AI supercharges laser physics with a stunning 250x speed boost
item.description: Researchers at Stanford, UCLA, and SLAC have developed an AI system that simulates complex laser interactions thousands of times faster than conventional methods. The breakthrough allows scientists to predict how laser pulses behave inside special crystals in just milliseconds, without sacrificing much accuracy. This could dramatically improve the precision and efficiency of powerful X-ray lasers used in cutting-edge scientific research.

item.title: Nature: Number of international students arriving in US plunges — worrying scientists
item.description: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03668-x Declines in students from China and India are driving the trend, which researchers say could slow the progress of US science.

item.title: New Scientist: Noise pollution is reshaping the health and behaviour of animals everywhere
item.description: There is almost nowhere on Earth free from disruptive human noise – but it's one of the easiest environmental problems to solve

item.title: New Scientist: Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?
item.description: The polar vortex winds have undergone an unprecedented weakening, which could bring cold weather to Europe. Some scientists suspect the record El Niño is to blame

item.title: New Scientist: Researchers build the first ever quantum clock that uses sunlight
item.description: Quantum clocks usually rely on advanced lasers and isolated atoms in the lab, but a new experiment showed that the same clock design can work with sunlight instead

item.title: New Scientist: Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?
item.description: We’ve loved sci-fi at New Scientist for the past 70 years, but which novels got the future right? From Neuromancer to The Handmaid’s Tale, Emily H. Wilson picks the most prescient reads of the past seven decades

item.title: Nature: This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03679-8 Being able to target and debug systems could improve artificial-intelligence safety and utility.

item.title: New Scientist: Think you know science? Try our quiz set by Nobel laureates
item.description: Test your knowledge of Nobel-prizewinning discoveries in microbiology, genomics and cosmology with questions set by the laureates themselves: Barry Marshall, Jennifer Doudna and Saul Perlmutter

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent
item.description: A new study reveals that viral infections may leave behind hidden damage to the immune system long after symptoms disappear. Researchers found that mice recovering from an acute infection experienced lasting changes to their spleens and weakened immune responses, potentially leaving them more vulnerable to future threats. Surprisingly, prior vaccination completely prevented these harmful changes in the mouse model.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy
item.description: A study of more than 750,000 pregnancies found that early exposure to Ozempic, Wegovy, and similar drugs was not linked to increased pregnancy complications when used for weight loss, but was associated with a higher risk of premature birth when prescribed for diabetes. The surprising difference suggests that diabetes itself may be driving the risk, although researchers caution that the drugs' safety during pregnancy remains uncertain.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch
item.description: A major study of nearly 1,900 older adults suggests that stopping statins after age 70 may be relatively safe in the short term for people who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke. However, a higher rate of serious cardiovascular events or death during longer follow-up raises questions about the risks of discontinuing these widely prescribed medications.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
item.description: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago
item.description: A mysterious force driving the expansion of the Universe may have undergone a dramatic reversal billions of years ago. Scientists exploring an overlooked branch of an alternative gravity theory discovered that dark energy could have switched from negative to positive roughly 9.5 billion years ago, potentially changing how we understand cosmic history.

item.title: ScienceDaily: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
item.description: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
item.description: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.

item.title: Nature: Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say
item.description: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03716-6 In the first of our new podcast series, a Nature reporter looks for reasons for hope in the face of overwhelming climate anxiety.

item.title: Nature: Chinese graduate students are now choosing to stay closer to home
item.description: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03456-7 Malaysia, Hong Kong and Macau are the new hot destinations for students.

item.title: Nature: Accept all changes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03516-y It’s the end — or is it?

item.title: New Scientist: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop
item.description: As we near Black Friday, columnist David Robson explores the psychology behind our impulse to buy things – and how marketers take advantage of our brains to push us to purchase

item.title: Nature: Found: a protein that drives ageing without unleashing inflammation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03638-3 Aged mice engineered to lack granzyme K have improved heart and liver function and less kidney damage.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue
item.description: Researchers have uncovered a surprising hidden function of a protein that may hold the key to repairing damaged muscles and treating muscular dystrophy. Known for protecting chromosomes, TRF2 also helps muscle stem cells maintain their identity and regenerate injured tissue. When scientists removed the protein in mice, muscles struggled to repair themselves, and muscular dystrophy progressed dramatically faster.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy
item.description: Researchers at Brown University have overcome a major obstacle to creating ultra-low-power computer chips that could help slash the energy demands of AI. Their breakthrough eliminates a long-standing "dead layer" problem that causes promising materials to stop working when made extremely thin. Remarkably, the new technique not only preserves the materials' electrical and magnetic properties at nearly atomic thicknesses but also gives them enhanced magnetic capabilities

item.title: ScienceDaily: Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that where men get their protein may be linked to their testosterone levels. Researchers studying more than 2,500 men found that higher animal protein intake, particularly from dairy, was associated with lower testosterone, while plant protein was linked to higher levels. The findings raise intriguing questions about how everyday food choices might relate to male hormone levels.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia were slower to switch strategies, less responsive to changes in difficulty, and less able to improve their approach over time. Distinct patterns of brain activity were linked to these difficulties and could even predict certain math-related abilities.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
item.description: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why
item.description: Colorectal cancer is making an alarming comeback in the United States after more than 20 years of declining rates, and the increase is no longer limited to younger adults. A major new study found rising rates across nearly every age group under 70, including older Americans who have historically benefited most from cancer screening.

item.title: ScienceDaily: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
item.description: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
item.description: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
item.description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
item.description: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

item.title: Nature: Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03705-9 Earlier CRISPR treatments require removal of a participant’s cells, a complex and costly approach.

item.title: New Scientist: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
item.description: AI-powered proof has rigorously proved that using quantum computers would not have huge advantages for a whole class of mathematical problems, confirming a vastly influential conjecture.

item.title: Nature: Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0 Insights into the reproductive modes of brown algae could help in the fight to protect them in warming climate.

item.title: Nature: Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z The Bundibugyo virus strain was circulating for weeks before its detection in May, but was missed owing to surveillance failures, testing gaps and funding cuts, researchers say.

item.title: New Scientist: A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time
item.description: Autonomous in-orbit manufacturing will be key to any future space economy, and researchers have taken the first step with a robot building a radio antenna without astronaut assistance

item.title: New Scientist: Economics, not climate summits, will dictate the net-zero transition
item.description: World leaders at COP31 show little enthusiasm for phasing out fossil fuels, but the plummeting costs of renewable energy will be the key factor in how quickly we can rein in global warming

item.title: Nature: This little brown mushroom is laced with a hallucinogen — and lethal toxins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03639-2 A Florida fungus might combine the psychedelic compound psilocybin with deadly chemicals to defend itself against hungry animals.

item.title: New Scientist: Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss
item.description: There is some evidence that pink noise signals can boost the brain's ability to clear out waste products. Now there are some indications that this might improve memory performance in people with Alzheimer's

item.title: Nature: Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03565-3 A global team profiled nearly 26 million brain cells from the basal ganglia to build a cross-species reference database that will help to understand conditions from Parkinson’s disease to addiction.

item.title: New Scientist: A little-known immune condition is being mistaken for food allergies
item.description: Doctors are calling for greater awareness of eosinophilic oseophagitis, a chronic condition that can cause symptoms similar to anaphylaxis

item.title: New Scientist: How Nvidia became so crucial to the AI boom
item.description: An espionage scandal has hit the biggest company in the world, and the fallout has the potential to destabilise economies that rely on its AI chips. Columnist Jacob Aron explains how Nvidia became the lynchpin to the AI industry

item.title: New Scientist: Vast data dump from Euclid space telescope reveals stunning galaxies
item.description: In the latest release of images collected by the Euclid space telescope, there are close-ups of distant galaxies where stars are in the process of forming

item.title: New Scientist: UK military taps up astronomers to spot snooping foreign satellites
item.description: The UK is unable to match the advanced surveillance and counter-surveillance programmes run by the US, China and Russia, but it is working with civilian astronomers to develop a way of monitoring spy satellites via ground-based telescopes

item.title: Nature: Author Correction: SLAMF6 as a drug-targetable suppressor of T cell immunity against cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11409-3 Author Correction: SLAMF6 as a drug-targetable suppressor of T cell immunity against cancer

item.title: Nature: RSV vaccines slash infections: data show jabs’ staggering success against dangerous virus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03573-3 Vaccines and monoclonal antibody injections are cutting hospitalizations for the respiratory virus.

item.title: Nature: Daily briefing: Should old, bad science be culled from the literature?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03675-y AI tools that summarize scientific literature are picking up decades-old flawed papers — should they be retracted? Plus, the first image of a black hole holds up to scrutiny and how the Artemis II mission might have disrupted GPS.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer
item.description: An NIH study found that women with high levels of two common “forever chemicals” had up to 93% higher rates of an aggressive form of breast cancer. The discovery raises concerns about the potential health effects of persistent chemicals found in everyday products.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
item.description: Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy release fructose that weakens the bonds holding neighboring tumor cells together, making it easier for cancer to spread. High dietary fructose levels and cholesterol-lowering statins also produced concerning effects in preclinical experiments.

item.title: ScienceDaily: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A groundbreaking new supercomputer simulation is revealing how the universe escaped its cosmic dark age and transformed into a cosmos filled with stars and galaxies. Called Lumina, it recreates 2 billion years of early cosmic history across a region 1.6 billion light-years wide, capturing extraordinary details that previous simulations could not.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
item.description: Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.

item.title: ScienceDaily: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields
item.description: NASA’s Parker Solar Probe has revealed a surprising secret hidden within the chaos of space: turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation when examined at extremely small scales. The discovery exposes an unexpected pattern in solar wind turbulence that could help scientists better understand solar activity and predict geomagnetic storms.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong
item.description: A surprising new study suggests that walking, jogging, and even traditional weight training may be less effective at stimulating bone formation than high-intensity sports involving explosive movements and sudden changes in direction. Researchers found that activities such as football and handball increased markers of bone formation by up to 46%, potentially revealing a better way to protect bones against aging and osteoporosis.

item.title: ScienceDaily: Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the first animals to venture onto land nearly 380 million years ago had surprisingly stiff necks, overturning a long-standing theory about evolution. Rather than evolving to help animals turn their heads, necks may have emerged as part of the anatomical changes that allowed them to move using their front limbs.
